headline.statement: A reported significance test in Experiment 1 uses more degrees of freedom than the paper's own stated sample size can produce -- the analysis it presents could not have been run on the sample it describes.
headline.evidence: "Female university (N = 47) students participated in the study for monetary compensation" and, for the contrast in question, "F(1, 46) = 6.95, p = 011" -- an error (denominator) degrees of freedom of 46. For any two-group comparison drawn from a fixed total sample, the maximum attainable error df is N-2; with the paper's own N=47 that ceiling is 45, one less than what is printed. The same experiment's other, larger 2x2 model already uses df=43 (e.g. F(1,43)=38.80), which is itself the largest df available from a 4-cell split of 47 participants -- so the single two-cell contrast cannot legitimately carry a larger df than the four-cell omnibus model.
headline.plain: The researchers describe recruiting 47 women for this study. But one of their key statistical tests reports using more "degrees of freedom" than 47 people can supply -- roughly speaking, the test claims to have compared more people than were ever in the room. The underlying p-value is fine on its own terms, but the sample size behind it is not real.

findings.title: Denominator degrees of freedom (df=46) exceeds the paper's own stated sample size (N=47)
findings.reported: "F(1, 46) = 6.95, p = 011" for the contrast between upward and downward comparison targets, in the unshared-birthday subset of a study explicitly described as "Female university (N = 47) students."
findings.computed: For any independent two-group split of a fixed total sample, maximum attainable error df = N-2. With the paper's own stated N=47, that ceiling is 45 -- one less than the printed df=46, and less than the 46 minimum participants (df+2) the printed value would require. The same experiment's own 4-cell 2x2 omnibus model (the largest model the design supports) uses df=43 throughout (F(1,43)=38.80; F(1,43)=7.77; F(1,43)=5.99) -- consistent with N=47 minus 4 cells -- so this single two-group contrast, drawn from at most half the sample, cannot legitimately exceed even that larger model's df, let alone the absolute N-2 ceiling. Re-running the F-to-p conversion (F=6.95, df1=1, df2=46) confirms the printed p=.011 is internally consistent with the printed F and df -- the arithmetic of the p-value is not the problem; the problem is that df=46 cannot have come from this sample.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own stated N=47 for Experiment 1 and the logically necessary bound df<=N-2 for any two-group comparison drawn from a fixed sample; no invented range or scale is used.
findings.plain: One of the paper's central results -- that participants who did not share a birthday with a comparison target responded symmetrically, the finding used to argue that ambiguous similarity information is necessary for the self-serving effect -- reports a statistical test drawn from more people than the study says it recruited. This is not a rounding slip; it is a number that cannot come from the sample as described, which means a reader cannot verify what test was actually run or trust the result attached to it.

consequence.explanation: This is the specific contrast supporting the paper's claim that self-serving responding requires ambiguous similarity information (Hypothesis 1, stated as a primary result). The printed p-value cannot be traced to a real sample, so this piece of evidence for the paper's central claim cannot be verified.

findings.title: Identical denominator df (124) recurs across four unrelated subgroup breakdowns in two different experiments with different total sample sizes
findings.location: Experiment 2 (Positive mood and Negative mood sections, N=141) and Experiment 4 (No load and Cognitive load sections, N=193)
findings.reported: Experiment 2: "in the positive mood conditions, direction of comparison, F(1, 124) = 14.79"; "presence of similarity cue... F(1, 124) = 18.61"; "interaction effect of direction of comparison and similarity information, F(1, 124) = 9.39"; and separately, "Among the negative mood conditions, only the main effect of direction was significant, F(1, 124) = 56.97." Experiment 4: "F(1,124) = 17.39"; "F(1,124) = 11.90"; "F(1,124) = 17.89"; "F(1,124) = 10.37"; "F(1,124) = 23.14"; "t(124) = -3.30"; "F(1,124) = 18.83"; "F(1,124) = 7.84."
findings.computed: Experiment 2's own internally consistent models establish a factorial-only sample of N=126 (the paper's df=118 omnibus model on the full 8-cell design implies N_factorial-8=118, i.e. N=126, leaving a control n of 15 against the total N=141 and its df=132 nine-condition model). The positive-mood-only and negative-mood-only subgroup tests, each drawn from a subset of that same 126-person factorial pool, both report the identical residual df=124 -- which, on a 2(direction)x2(cue) model (4 parameters), implies a subgroup n of 128 for EACH mood group. Two subgroups of 128 people cannot both be drawn from a shared pool of 126: even a single subgroup of 128 already exceeds the entire factorial sample. The identical value 124 is then reused, unexplained, for eight further tests across a wholly different experiment (Experiment 4, total N=193, its own factorial-only omnibus using df=110).
findings.assumptions: Assumes the positive-mood-only and negative-mood-only tests use a standard multi-parameter ANOVA model (direction x cue) rather than an undocumented pooled-error contrast scheme; the paper does state it used single-df pooled contrasts (citing Jaccard 1998) for its explicit control-condition comparisons (the F(1,132)/F(1,132) tests), so an unreported variant of that same pooling scheme applied instead to these mood-subset breakdowns cannot be entirely ruled out, which is why this stops short of impossible.
findings.plain: The number of participants behind a statistical test is supposed to change when you change the group being tested. Here, the exact same denominator (124) appears for a breakdown of positive-mood participants and, separately, for a breakdown of negative-mood participants in the same experiment -- and then again for entirely different breakdowns in an unrelated experiment with a different total number of participants. Under the sample sizes the paper itself reports elsewhere, this value cannot arise honestly from either subgroup. This bears directly on the tests that support three of the paper's four central hypotheses.

findings.title: Two significant p-values print without their leading decimal point
findings.reported: "F(1, 46) = 6.95, p = 011" and "F(1, 110) = 11.23, p = 001" (both missing the leading decimal that would read p = .011 and p = .001).
findings.computed: Recalculating F(1,46)=6.95 gives p=.0114, consistent with the intended .011 reading; the second instance sits alongside a df already found to be irreconcilable with the paper's stated N (see rank 1). Both are typesetting defects rather than arithmetic errors on their own.
findings.assumptions: None beyond ordinary APA decimal notation; treated as a proofreading slip, not a computational one.
findings.plain: Two of the paper's reported p-values are missing their decimal point (printed as "011" instead of ".011"). Read the intended way, the numbers are fine. On its own this is an ordinary proofreading slip -- but one of the two sentences it appears in is also the sentence carrying the impossible degrees-of-freedom problem above, which is worth noting even though it proves nothing by itself.

findings.title: No table or experiment reports per-cell sample sizes, blocking GRIM/GRIMMER verification of every mean and SD
findings.location: Table 1 (Experiment 2, 8 cells) and Table 2 (Experiment 3, 16 cells); all four experiments generally
findings.reported: Both tables print mean (SD) on stated, printable scales (a single seven-point self-evaluation item; a three-item nine-point similarity composite), but neither the tables nor the surrounding text state a per-cell or per-condition n anywhere in the paper -- only total experiment N and various ANOVA error degrees of freedom.
findings.computed: check_table was run against both tables' 24 mean/SD cells; grim_check, grimmer_check and sprite_reconstruct all refused for want of a per-cell n, which error df alone cannot supply without assuming perfectly balanced cells (an assumption the instructions direct against making).
findings.assumptions: None -- this is a refusal to check, not a finding about the numbers themselves.
findings.plain: The paper's two summary tables report averages and spreads for each experimental group, but never say how many people were in each group -- only the total for the whole experiment. That gap means the paper's most checkable numbers (the individual cell means) cannot be verified at all, in either direction. This is a reporting gap, not evidence of a problem with the numbers themselves.

not_checked.reason: No per-cell or per-condition sample size is reported anywhere in the paper, so GRIM/GRIMMER/SPRITE cannot be run on these stated-scale (1-7) single-item means without assuming an unstated per-cell n.
Same missing-per-cell-n limitation as Table 1. The Similarity row is additionally a 3-item composite mean, which this toolkit's GRIM/GRIMMER cannot correctly evaluate even with n known.

not_checked.location: Pilot study mood and self-evaluation composite indices
not_checked.reason: Both are multi-item composite means (4 items; 3 items); this toolkit's granularity checks model single-item integer data, not k-item composites, and per-group n is not reported either.

No experiment reports the number of participants in each factorial cell; only total N and various ANOVA error degrees of freedom are given, which do not determine individual cell sizes without assuming balance.

not_checked.location: Pairwise p-values reported only as thresholds (e.g. 'p < .001', 'ps > .84')
not_checked.reason: A large share of the paper's p-values are reported only as bounds without an exact value or accompanying test statistic sufficient for further recomputation.

limitations: Figures were not read in this stage; Stage 1 examined all three figures with extract_figures and found none carries a numeric value not already printed in the text or tables, and that finding is carried forward here without independent re-verification of the images.

No per-cell or per-condition sample sizes are reported anywhere in this paper, which blocks GRIM/GRIMMER/SPRITE verification of every individual mean and SD in Tables 1 and 2 -- the paper's most granular, and otherwise most checkable, numbers.

This paper carries a journal-issued retraction header and is one of the works covered by the Levelt Committee's finding of fabricated data by co-author Diederik Stapel; that background is noted for context but is not itself evidence for any specific finding above, each of which rests on the paper's own printed numbers.

questions_for_authors.question: Could you supply the exact analytic model (including the number of participants) used for the F(1, 46) = 6.95 contrast in Experiment 1's unshared-birthday self-evaluations, and separately for the F(1, 124) tests reported in Experiment 2's positive-mood and negative-mood sections and in Experiment 4's no-load and cognitive-load sections?
